name: Calcium hydroxide relaxer

card.summary: The 'no-lye' relaxer, billed as gentler on sensitive scalps than lye; no study has shown a different health profile.
card.note: Can still cause burns and breakage; health studies do not separate it from lye relaxers.

lead: A calcium hydroxide relaxer, sold as a "no-lye" relaxer, is a chemical hair straightener used to turn tight curls or coils into smoother, straighter hair. Its active agent is guanidine hydroxide, formed when a calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) cream is mixed with a guanidine carbonate activating solution just before use. [1][2]

Like other relaxers, it permanently alters treated hair by breaking the disulfide bonds that hold the curl, so new growth stays curly and needs retouching. [2][3] Wikipedia describes lye relaxers as containing 5 to 10 percent sodium hydroxide at a pH of 10 to 14, and the no-lye group as milder alkalis including potassium, lithium or guanidine hydroxide; products of this kind are positioned for sensitive scalps. [1][3]

Wikipedia cautions that scalp burns can occur with lye and no-lye relaxers if the scalp is overexposed, and that contact dermatitis is possible. [1] Studies of relaxer use and health outcomes do not separate calcium-based products from sodium hydroxide ones. [1]

chain: Alkaline cream breaks disulfide bonds in the hair shaft
Straighter, smoother hair that new growth gradually reveals
angle.text: The treatment straightens tightly curled hair for easier styling and a sleeker look, lasting until the hair grows out. No-lye products are chosen by people who want a milder-feeling relaxer on a sensitive scalp.

infobox: Guanidine hydroxide, from calcium hydroxide plus guanidine carbonate [1]

paras: The calcium hydroxide cream and guanidine carbonate activating solution are combined shortly before use, generating guanidine hydroxide, which Wikipedia describes as a weaker alkali than sodium hydroxide. [1] The alkali breaks disulfide bonds in the hair keratin similarly to lye products. [1][2]

Other no-lye approaches include potassium or lithium hydroxide, ammonium thioglycolate, which must be oxidized afterward, and ammonium sulfite or bisulfite in home kits that are weaker and slower. [1] Relaxers are generally suited to coarse, tight curls. [2]

Garrett Augustus Morgan is credited by Wikipedia with discovering a hair-straightening cream by accident in 1909. Lye relaxers went on sale in 1917, and the first commercial no-lye relaxer, using potassium hydroxide, followed in 1919. [1] Straightening was very popular in the 1950s, and Madam C. J. Walker popularized the straightening comb in the early 1900s. [3]
In the 1990s the Rio Hair Naturalizer System, marketed as chemical-free, was associated with scalp damage and hair loss, led to a class action and was withdrawn. [1]

Both lye and no-lye relaxers can cause scalp burns, irritant or allergic dermatitis and hair breakage. A petroleum-jelly base is often applied to the scalp beforehand. [1] No separate risk profile for calcium hydroxide products is given. [1]

Wikipedia also reports health studies on relaxer use generally: a 2012 cohort of more than 22,000 African-American women found an association with uterine fibroids, a 2022 NIH analysis of more than 33,000 women reported nearly doubled uterine cancer risk among frequent users of hair-straightening products, and a 2017 study found women using chemical relaxers were nearly twice as likely to develop breast cancer. [1][3] In 2023 the FDA proposed banning formaldehyde as a relaxer ingredient. [1] These studies did not analyse by alkali type. [1]
No studies specific to calcium hydroxide relaxers were identified. Studies of relaxer use generally, described above, did not compare the two alkali types. [1]

quick.overview:
A calcium hydroxide relaxer is the 'no-lye' alternative to the traditional sodium hydroxide cream, used to straighten tightly curled hair. It is mixed with a guanidine activator before use.

It is often marketed toward people with sensitive scalps.
quick.mechanism: Calcium hydroxide and guanidine carbonate react to form guanidine hydroxide, a weaker alkali that breaks the hair's disulfide bonds.
quick.risks: Burns, dermatitis and breakage are reported for both lye and no-lye relaxers. Observational health studies have not separated product types, and cosmetics are not pre-approved by the FDA.
